[Conditional Logic | LR](https://app.lsatlab.com/video-library/?videoid=16784), Patrick Tyrrell, published 2020-07-28. Observed Vimeo embed: 438082783. Parent verified player runtime 24:34. Caption source: `raw/sources/lsat-lab-lectures/16784/source.en-US.vtt`, native en-US track. No audio playback or board inspection is claimed.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Source summary\\r\\n\\r\\nThe lesson begins with rule meaning and four possible fact positions, establishing valid triggering and invalid reversal/negation. Contraposition expands immediately to compound conditions. Chaining then contrasts rule conclusions with factual conclusions, including a partly satisfied compound trigger. Translation follows these operations: certainty, requirements, indicator direction, negative universals, exception language, and biconditionals. Training uses rhetorical inference questions, two explicit early pause tasks, equivalent translations, and a ten-item pause-and-solve worksheet with an indicator reference. The instructor reviews each item’s indicator, diagram direction, negation, and contrapositive. Later items demand interpretation beyond the memorized list and compound negation. The closing prioritizes indicator fluency, contraposition, compound negation, and avoiding invalid moves. Automated feedback, timed practice, mastery checks, and actual LSAT question IDs are absent from the captions. Quantifiers receive a brief translation aside, not a full treatment.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Chronological factual topic ledger\\r\\n\\r\\nTimes identify approximate teaching transitions in overlapping subtitle cues. Entries are topic labels and observed activity metadata.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Time | Topic | Observed training format |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| 00:10–00:31 | Objectives | Introduction |\\r\\n| 00:31–01:02 | Arrow; certainty; sufficient/necessary | Concrete rule |\\r\\n| 01:02–01:41 | Positive trigger; absent trigger | Contrasting cases |\\r\\n| 01:41–02:31 | Positive consequent; reversal; flaw | Contrast and warning |\\r\\n| 02:31–02:58 | Absent consequent | Inference question |\\r\\n| 02:58–04:05 | Contraposition; invalid negation | Explanation |\\r\\n| 04:05–04:37 | Compound antecedent; AND/OR negation | Symbolic demonstration |\\r\\n| 04:37–05:14 | Compound consequent contraposition | Explicit pause; worked answer |\\r\\n| 05:14–05:45 | Rule conclusion versus fact conclusion | Task distinction |\\r\\n| 05:45–06:37 | Three-rule chains; intermediate inferences | Worked symbolic chain |\\r\\n| 06:37–07:11 | Disjunctive outcome with eliminating fact | Worked symbolic inference |\\r\\n| 07:11–07:53 | Partly satisfied conjunction; residual conditional | Explicit pause; worked answer |\\r\\n| 07:53–09:05 | Certainty; universals; guarantees; requirements | Recognition and requirement rephrasing |\\r\\n| 09:05–09:29 | Equivalent wording | Pause to inspect slide examples |\\r\\n| 09:29–10:19 | Indicator columns; semantic categories | Reference list |\\r\\n| 10:19–11:45 | Negative universal | Plausibility contrast; alternate translations |\\r\\n| 11:45–12:53 | Negative quantifier rephrasing | Brief comparison |\\r\\n| 12:53–14:49 | Unless/until/without | Two equivalent approaches; simple examples |\\r\\n| 14:49–16:29 | Exception language with compounds | Parentheses; negation; alternate formulation |\\r\\n| 16:29–17:51 | Biconditional indicators | Two arrows versus same-status cases |\\r\\n| 17:51–18:48 | Otherwise; explicit opposite rule | Worked interpretation |\\r\\n| 18:48–19:29 | Ten-item worksheet instructions | Reference aid; pause; translation plus contraposition |\\r\\n| 19:29–19:49 | Item 1: when | Answer review |\\r\\n| 19:49–20:15 | Item 2: implies | Answer review |\\r\\n| 20:15–20:32 | Item 3: no | Answer review |\\r\\n| 20:32–20:49 | Item 4: each | Answer review |\\r\\n| 20:49–21:18 | Item 5: unless | Two approaches |\\r\\n| 21:18–21:53 | Item 6: never | Unlisted-word interpretation |\\r\\n| 21:53–22:19 | Item 7: any; alternative will reading | Scope and ambiguity |\\r\\n| 22:19–22:39 | Item 8: only | Answer review |\\r\\n| 22:39–23:18 | Item 9: without plus AND | Compound negation; alternate approach |\\r\\n| 23:18–23:42 | Item 10: prerequisite | Unlisted-word interpretation |\\r\\n| 23:42–24:20 | Fluency goals | Recap |\\r\\n| 24:20–24:35 | Outro | End material |\\r\\n\\r\\nNo proprietary worksheet sentences or answer bank are reproduced here.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Original analysis: prerequisites and learning demand\\r\\n\\r\\nThis compact lesson assumes the learner can handle abstract letters and elementary negation almost immediately. It introduces AND/OR contraposition approximately four minutes in, before detailed indicator translation. That makes it useful as a compressed overview or refresher; a ground-up independent pathway would benefit from more isolated practice before the combined tasks. This judgment concerns instructional demand, not evidence of learner outcomes.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe four fact-position cases teach an important boundary: from S→N, S licenses N and ¬N licenses ¬S; ¬S and N alone leave the other term undetermined. Students must interpret uncertainty as an answer rather than feel compelled to infer something.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe linking section requires a different output type from triggering. Rules alone yield another relationship. Adding a fact can yield a factual consequence. A fact satisfying part of an AND antecedent can also simplify the remaining conditional demand. This last operation merits its own assignable skill in LSAT U rather than being hidden under general linking.\\r\\n\\r\\nTranslation strategy is partly syntactic and partly semantic. The reference identifies arrow placement, but unlisted words and equivalent requirement readings require understanding necessity. The lesson therefore does not justify teaching indicator memorization as sufficient mastery.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe practice sequence shifts from guided cases to a mixed worksheet and delayed instructor review. This is feedback through worked explanation after the student pauses. Captions provide no evidence of answer entry, immediate adaptive feedback, a scored diagnostic, retries with fresh items, or gating. A ten-item mixed worksheet is one observed training event, not a complete inventory of LSAT Lab exercises.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Original LSAT U examples and assignable skills\\r\\n\\r\\nAll examples below are new and are not paraphrases of source exercises.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Fact positions:** every licensed pilot has passed an exam. Test separately what follows from licensed, not licensed, passed, and not passed.\\r\\n- **Compound contraposition:** inspected AND sealed → dispatchable. If not dispatchable, at least one prerequisite failed. Students must not infer both failed.\\r\\n- **Rule versus fact:** regional → registered; registered → approved. Derive regional → approved. Only after a named applicant is regional may the student derive that applicant’s approval.\\r\\n- **Residual condition:** code AND badge → entry; entry → attendance. Given the badge, code → attendance still remains conditional until a code fact is supplied.\\r\\n- **Equivalent exception translations:** equipment operates only when a safety check has passed. Require both a necessity reading and its contrapositive.\\r\\n- **Biconditional scope:** a display lights exactly when the circuit is active. Contrast an explicitly given two-way rule with an unsupported reversal of a one-way rule.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor Joshua\'s Beginner/Medium/Advanced model, start with a single operation, then mix operations, then vary language and compounds. Use a separate general mixed assignment at each level. These are design proposals, not LSAT Lab\'s observed level definitions.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Nuances and source-fidelity limits\\r\\n\\r\\nThe short negative-quantifier aside includes few, most, and not-all transformations. In LSAT U, define the intended mathematical meaning of few before equating it with most-not; everyday usage can be vague. No existence assumption should be silently imported into a universal rule. The captions do not give a full quantifier inference lesson.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe certainty discussion includes guaranteed causal wording. LSAT U should distinguish the logical guarantee encoded by a sentence from proof of causation in an argument. The lesson\'s broad certainty framing is a recognition heuristic, not a complete account of every kind of statement.\\r\\n\\r\\nOtherwise creates a biconditional in the discussed case because the other branch supplies the opposite outcome. It should not be taught as automatically biconditional in every sentence.\\r\\n\\r\\nNative-track labeling does not establish transcription accuracy. Captions contain obvious substitutions involving contrapositive, flaw, letters, names, and ordinary nouns. One compound explanation labels the inferred side inconsistently; diagrams are necessary to verify its intended symbols. The item with alternative any/will readings requires the unseen sentence and subject scope to adjudicate fully. The slide\'s complete indicator list, displayed diagrams, and exact written worksheet were not recovered by reading captions. Do not fill these gaps from guesses.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Coverage check\\r\\n\\r\\nAll 573 numbered cues were read from opening to final cue; the initially truncated middle was read separately. First cue: 00:02.960. Final cue: 24:33.080–24:35.140. Only gaps greater than two seconds are the initial 2.960-second lead-in and 6.030 seconds before the final outro cue. Overlapping cues are normal here. Final timestamp exceeds the observed 24:34 runtime by 1.140 seconds; preserve this mismatch rather than trimming the source.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis establishes complete coverage of the supplied caption stream and its teaching sequence. It does not establish audiovisual fidelity, complete board content, or a complete LSAT Lab curriculum.\\r\\n\\r\\n## 2026-10-02 public video review and opening correction\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua rejected the local first page: it asked what a rule tells the student before explaining what conditionals are or why they matter. This supersedes acceptance of the earlier opening preview; tests and visual checks did not establish teaching quality.\\r\\n\\r\\nReviewed Patrick\'s official public [Conditional Logic | LSAT Logical Reasoning](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jeDnykOrswY), observed runtime 24:34. Full exported auto-generated English caption stream covers 00:02 through 24:33. Read every caption. A read-only comparison found all 573 caption texts match the earlier archived lesson 16784 exactly. This verifies public-video identity with the prior caption analysis. No separate LSAT Loud title has been established; that wording is treated as a likely dictation reference to LSAT Lab, not verified product metadata.\\r\\n\\r\\nFresh browser visual inspection adds evidence beyond the prior caption-only review:\\r\\n\\r\\n- 01:05: the same NYC/USA rule has a separate Linda fact and a question before the conclusion is shown.\\r\\n- 01:10: the conclusion is revealed beside that fact; the original relationship remains visible.\\r\\n- 01:25: an absent trigger is contrasted with an unknown outcome; the board explicitly permits either outcome.\\r\\n- 02:40: a separate contrapositive board reverses and negates the two terms. This was viewed, not imported into the introductory lesson.\\r\\n- 09:04: a requirement reading and combined requirement chain are on the board.\\r\\n- 09:14: equivalent expression families are grouped on a reference board, following the explicit pause instruction at about 09:05.\\r\\n- 19:19: an indicator reference is available during the pause-and-diagram instructions before answer explanations.\\r\\n\\r\\nScreenshots are in visual-proof/ with the lab-primer prefix and timestamps. The 01:05 filename was initially captured after a keyboard Home shortcut accidentally reset playback; it was corrected by seeking back and verifying both media currentTime 65 and displayed 1:05 before saving. No invalid frame is offered as proof. Source screenshots are private research evidence, not student lesson assets. No full real-time audio watch or precise silence-duration measurement is claimed.\\r\\n\\r\\nExplicit pause requests from the captions occur around 04:39, 07:11, 09:05 and 19:16. Earlier rhetorical questions and staged visual reveals establish question-before-answer progression, not a verified multi-second silent pause.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe design pattern to adapt is one relationship, one changed fact, a learner-controlled thinking interval, then the explanation and a contrasting mistake. The video itself introduces abstract symbols and contraposition quickly. Joshua\'s requested first page should be slower: what a condition means; what a conditional statement connects; why this matters on the LSAT; certainty compared with usual likelihood; one fully explained original example; then a pause before applying it. Sufficient/necessary terminology and indicator families belong after this introduction. The original LSAT U ready/packed example can remain after this foundation, rather than serving as a substitute for the definition.\\r\\n"}'}]

Joshua assigns the appropriate lesson or practice; a student sees that assigned work.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Order | What we teach, in sequence | What the learner does here |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| **1. What a conditional tells you** | Define a condition as an idea that can be true or false. Define a conditional through if/then. Explain what the relationship lets us know and why that matters for LSAT conclusions. Read one original rule naturally. Explain that must rules out an exception to the stated relationship. if-left/then-right; arrow means certainty; sufficient trigger and necessary outcome | Explain conditional meaning and the two roles; introduce symbols only at the approved notation stage |\n| 1:02–2:46 | Four fact positions; positive trigger works; absent trigger leaves outcome open; positive outcome does not establish trigger; absent outcome rules out trigger | Preserve the same rule while changing one fact; let students answer unknown |\n| 2:46–3:48 | Contrapositive; reverse and negate; reject reverse and inverse | Later conceptual then symbolic contraposition within the approved source-order skeleton |\n| 3:48–5:02 | Compound contraposition; AND/OR changes; learner pause | Keep in later compound lessons; pause on equivalent expressions | Explain multiple formulations of one relationship, then give an untimed think interval |\n| 9:18–10:18 | Attached idea goes on its indicated side; cluster words; learn the meaning of a requirement even when its wording is unfamiliar | Full idea selection, grammar-sensitive placement, required idea on the right |\n| 10:18 | Begins negative-universal explanation | Scope boundary: no-statements require separate negation mechanics |\n\nThe local [approved content-order skeleton](../../brainstorms/2026-09-30-conditional-curriculum/2026-10-02-opening-lessons-source-map.md) remains the authoring backbone. The two roles sit with their ideas. |\n| 055656 | Geographic example; if left, then right | Words are read as a relationship, not two unrelated labels. The original arrow stays visible while the invalid inference is tested. |\n| 055817 | Four available-inference rows | Positive sufficient and negative necessary support conclusions; negative sufficient and positive necessary produce question marks. |\n| 055846 | Given left→right; negated right→negated left | Both roles reverse and both truth values change in the contrapositive. |\n| 055945 | Three-rule chain with unanswered conditional | Prompt appears before the answer. Rules alone ask for another conditional relationship. |\n| 060020 | Same chain with endpoint and contrapositive answers | Learner sees the answer after attempting the prior question. |\n| 060104 | Whole chain and reversed negated chain | Intermediate terms remain visible while endpoint inference is summarized. |\n| 060229 | Four certainty categories under A→B | Rules/principles, universals, guarantees/causes, requirements are language forms of the same directed relationship. A causal assertion's form is not evidence that causation is established. |\n| 060217 | A requires B; two requirements in ordinary language | Requirement readback is the teaching bridge. The admissions example is illustrative wording, not an empirically verified admissions rule to reuse. |\n| 060311 | Equivalent wording grouped into four families | If/when/whenever; universals; outcome-guarantee forms; requirement forms express the same relation despite different sentence order. The table includes negative and exception forms outside the simple Group 1/2 scope. |\n| 060411 | Complete left/right keyword reference, grouped by function | Captures the previously missing board inventory. Its **right** inventory is: ensures, implies, leads to, will, always; only, only if, requires, must, necessitates, depends on, relies on, unless, until, without. These are the vendor's observed labels, not an unconditional parsing algorithm and not Joshua's complete group taxonomy.\n\nFor the ordinary Group 1/2 work, adapt the rule/universal and requirement/guarantee meanings, preserving the full qualified idea attached to an expression. Sentence location does not determine diagram side. In an if sentence, the if-clause may come first or last. In a requirement sentence, the goal can come before the required thing or after it. Teach students to identify what is enough and what that situation requires, then read the whole relationship back.\n\nKeep **no** and **unless/until/without** in their separately taught negative/exception lessons. Their appearance in the reference does not eliminate the additional transformations. **Only** and **the only** require separate grammatical explanations. **Always**, **will**, and **must** must be read within the actual sentence: a rule prescribing an action is not proof that someone complied. The source's equivalent-expression board makes these distinctions worth teaching with controlled contrasts.\n\n## What to adapt and what to correct\n\nUse original examples and wording. Useful design patterns are: stable rule plus one changed fact; full-idea labels; prompt before reveal; role labels next to terms; original and contrapositive side by side after the meaning is understood; equivalent sentences before a reference table; and a final meaning-based check rather than keyword recitation alone.\n\nDo not copy the clip's introductory numerical prevalence claims into course copy. No supporting study is supplied. Do not repeat the caption's statement that the rule disappears when the sufficient condition is absent: the rule still holds, but that fact alone leaves the other condition unsettled. Do not imply this ten-minute overview proves mastery or teaches all conditional skills.\n\nNo fresh real-time video watch or audio review occurred in this ingest.
